rejected.title: Country in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander writing
card: Country is more than land. For many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, it includes land, waters, sky, plants, animals and stories, and it is tied to culture, identity and belonging.
Many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander writers use imagery, symbol and metaphor drawn from Country and Place. A river, a tree or a star may carry ideas about family, memory, law or connection.
Read these images as part of a living culture, not as decoration. Ask what the image shows about the speaker's relationship to Country, and avoid treating it as just a pretty setting.
Be careful not to claim one meaning for all communities. Nations have their own languages, stories and places, so use the text's own details and say what the writer shows, rather than guessing.
rejected.remember: In this writing, images of Country often express culture, identity and belonging, so read them with respect and from the evidence in the text.

a.q: A poet describes a gum tree as holding her family's stories in its roots. How should a respectful reader take this image?
opts: As a symbol of belonging, linking family and Country
As decoration that adds a pleasant bush setting
As proof that all communities see trees the same way
As a plain fact about how deep tree roots grow
a.why: The image links the tree to family stories, so it expresses belonging to Country. Treating it as decoration is tempting, but it ignores the relationship the image shows between people and Country.
a.clue: Ask what the image says about the speaker's connection to Country.

b.q: A student writes: 'The river in this poem means the same thing in every Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander text.' What is the best response?
opts: Meanings differ, so base the reading on the poem's details
It is correct, because Country always means the same
It is correct, because rivers are symbols of life only
Meanings do not matter, so the river can be ignored
b.why: Nations and writers have different languages, stories and places, so a reading should come from the details of the text. The claim of one meaning for all is tempting because Country is important to many writers, but it treats very different cultures as one.
b.clue: Think about whether one meaning could suit many different Nations.

version.title: Country in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander writing
card: For many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, Country is the land, waters, sky and living things they belong to. It holds culture, family and stories.
Many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander writers draw imagery, symbol and metaphor from Country and Place. A waterhole, a reef or a star can carry ideas about identity, memory and belonging.
Reading respectfully means treating these images as part of a living culture, not as scenery. Ask what each image shows about the speaker's relationship with Country and community.
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples include many communities, each with its own languages and stories. Base a reading on the text's own details, not on one meaning assumed for all.
version.remember: Images of Country can express culture, identity and belonging, so read them with respect and from the text's own details.

a.q: In a poem, the speaker says the reef remembers her grandfather's songs. What is the most respectful way to read this image?
opts: As a sign of the bond between family, culture and sea
As scenery that adds colour to a tropical setting
As a fact about the sounds that coral reefs make
As a meaning shared by every First Nations writer
a.why: The image ties the reef to the grandfather's songs, so it expresses a living connection between family, culture and sea Country. Reading it as scenery is tempting, but it ignores that relationship.
a.clue: What does the image link the reef to?

b.q: A student's essay claims a river image means exactly the same thing in every Aboriginal writer's work. What is the strongest correction?
opts: Peoples and texts differ, so read from this poem's details
The river is scenery, so its meaning is not worth reading
Rivers stand for life, so that meaning fits every text
The poet's background has no bearing on the image
b.why: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples include many communities with their own languages and stories, so one meaning cannot be assumed for all. A strong reading comes from the poem's own details. Saying rivers stand for life in every text makes the same mistake as the student.
b.clue: Could one meaning suit many different peoples?
